content: Serum sickness is a hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in response to an antiserum derived from an animal source. It is classified as a type III hypersensitivity reaction, which involves immune complex formation. Unlike anaphylaxis, the symptoms of serum sickness do not appear immediately. The condition arises when the immune system identifies the animal-derived proteins in the antiserum as foreign antigens. In response, the body produces antibodies that bind to these proteins, forming immune complexes. These immune complexes can deposit in tissues and trigger an inflammatory response, leading to the symptoms associated with serum sickness. In addition to antisera, certain medications, such as penicillin-based drugs and lincomycin hydrochloride, can also induce serum sickness. Common clinical features include skin rashes, joint pain (arthralgia), fever, and swelling of the lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy). Treatment for serum sickness is often supportive, as the symptoms typically resolve on their own over time. However, in severe cases, corticosteroids may be prescribed to reduce inflammation. Antihistamines can also be used to alleviate symptoms such as rash and itching.
